findings.title: The Step-0 import design was narrowed to the CLI's restriction instead of the CLI being fixed
locations: instruments/audit-changes/PROTOCOL.md is unaffected; the promise lived only in §8
findings.before: "them, and `import.json` (§6.1). It needs no `.gbg/config.toml` — the one `round` verb that runs before `init`; `self verify` still precedes it — and refuses (exit 2) an existing target round"
findings.after: "them, and `import.json` (§6.1). It is to run before `init`, on a tree with no `.gbg/config.toml` — which the CLI does not yet allow, since `cmd_round` reads the config before dispatching any round verb, and the implemented `--empty` path calls neither `guard` nor `self verify`, unlike every other round verb."
findings.why_it_matters: `gbg round import --empty` is the ONE Step-0 verb that is built (Rounds.jl:736), and its whole purpose is a legacy pile on a tree that has not been `init`ed. Rounds.jl:856 calls `Config.read()` before any round verb dispatches, so on such a tree it throws ConfigError and returns 2 — the verb cannot be used in the only scenario it exists for. Faced with that, the edit amended the design to say the CLI "does not yet allow" it rather than moving the config read past the import branch (a two-line change: dispatch `import --empty` before `cfg = Config.read()`). The same sentence also strikes the design's own precondition, "`self verify` still precedes it", because `import_empty` does not call it — so the guarantee that the running copy is the pinned one is now documented away for this verb rather than supplied. Both halves move the text toward the code, and the operator who reads §8 after this diff will no longer know a capability was owed.
findings.description: A design promise that `round import` needs no config and runs before `init` was rewritten, in the same window that documents the verb as NOT YET BUILT, into a statement that the CLI does not allow it. The restriction is real (Rounds.jl:856 reads the config for every round verb) and cheap to lift for the one implemented `--empty` path; the change set recorded it as design instead. The companion clause `self verify still precedes it` was dropped for the same reason — the implemented path omits the call. Nothing that worked stopped working; what changed is that the owed behaviour is no longer owed in writing.
findings.evidence: base: "It needs no `.gbg/config.toml` — the one `round` verb that runs before `init`; `self verify` still precedes it"; head: "which the CLI does not yet allow, since `cmd_round` reads the config before dispatching any round verb, and the implemented `--empty` path calls neither `guard` nor `self verify`"; code: Rounds.jl:856 `cfg = Config.read()` above every `verb == ...` branch, and import_empty (736-755) contains no `guard(` and no `self_verify(`.

findings.title: RULE.INST.CARRY's new CARRY_LIMIT clause names the release refusal and hides the close refusal
findings.before: "... it is re-banked there, never rediscovered, and a final release refuses while a carried blocker or major stands or the backlog is not draining."
findings.after: "... it is re-banked there, never rediscovered, and a final release refuses while a carried blocker or major stands, while anything has been carried CARRY_LIMIT (3) times, or while the backlog is not draining."
findings.why_it_matters: This statement is the rendered fleet policy every consumer reads at its pinned version. As amended it places the CARRY_LIMIT consequence at the RELEASE, which reads as "carrying a fourth time is allowed, only the release complains". The code refuses far earlier and harder: `carry_conditions` pushes `--carry $id: carried 3× already (limit 3) — this is not a deferral any more; escalate it` and that check is NOT gated on `at_cap`, so a round whose pass budget is spent and whose only remaining exit is to carry a 3×-carried finding cannot close at all until the owner adjudicates or escalates. An owner following the amended sentence will plan a close that `gbg round close` refuses.
findings.description: The edit set out to make the rule statement current about CARRY_LIMIT and made it current in one direction only. Release.jl:46 does refuse at `carries >= CARRY_LIMIT`, so the added clause is not wrong; but the refusal that bites first — close's own, at Passes.jl:1086, unconditional on the pass budget — is still unstated, and the sentence now reads as though closing over a 3×-carried finding is available. The rule's own `check` is `test:test/rounds.jl`, whose CARRY_LIMIT case (test/rounds.jl:577-578) exercises the close refusal, so the behaviour the statement omits is the one the check actually pins.
findings.evidence: Passes.jl:1086-1087 `e === nothing || Int(e["carries"]) < CARRY_LIMIT || push!(fails, "--carry $id: carried $(e["carries"])× already (limit $CARRY_LIMIT) — this is not a deferral any more; escalate it")`, reached for every id in `carry` with no `at_cap` escape, versus the amended statement's "a final release refuses ... while anything has been carried CARRY_LIMIT (3) times".

findings.title: The prose-span guard dropped the `of` exemption that no defect implicated
locations: test/coverage.jl:117-123 (the rationale comment added with it)
findings.why_it_matters: The defect that was paid for was the English preposition "in": both unescaped spans, in verify-act.js and verify-state.js, read "one object per lane in `lane_files`". Removing `(?<!of )` as well takes a JavaScript form with it: `for (const x of `abc`)` — a non-interpolated template literal iterated directly — was accepted by this guard before and now turns `Pkg.test()` red, as does a bare backtick after "of" inside an ordinary single-quoted JS string (`description: 'one of `a` or `b`'`), which is valid JavaScript that closes nothing. The exposure is small and the authors measured it ("no such form occurs in the eleven scripts or the prelude"), and I confirmed it: running the head regex over all eleven scripts plus instruments/prelude.js with comments stripped as the test strips them yields zero matches. Filed as a nit because the widening is real but currently costs nothing, and the workaround (escape the backtick) exists.
findings.description: One of the two exemptions removed was implicated in the BLOCKER (`in`), the other was not (`of`), and the commit removes both. The test's own comment concedes the second: "Neither operator is ever followed by a template literal in these scripts" and "no such form occurs in the eleven scripts or the prelude (checked 2026-09-12)" — i.e. the `of` exemption protected nothing and, symmetrically, its removal catches nothing that exists. This is a guard made wider than the defect required, on a frozen-script surface where every future edit must pass it. Note a side effect neither the comment nor the new assertions mention: because the lookbehinds match the last three characters and not a word, `(?<!in )` and `(?<!of )` had also been exempting every word ENDING in "in " or "of " ("within", "again", "proof"), so the tightening is broader than the two keywords named.
findings.evidence: Removed from the regex: `(?<!in )(?<!of )`. The commit's own justification, added at test/coverage.jl:121-122: "Neither operator is ever followed by a template literal in these scripts — the forms are `x in obj` and `for (const x of [...])` — so the exemption protected nothing"; and at 192-193: "no such form occurs in the eleven scripts or the prelude (checked 2026-09-12), and a guard forced to choose should keep the defect that has actually happened over the one that has not." My own re-run of the head regex over the eleven scripts and the prelude, comments stripped: no matches.
